content.text: A static site whose pages are Content documents in its own git repository, and whose authors edit those pages in the built site itself. There is no CMS server, no database and no user table: the repository is the source of truth, a save is a commit, and the commit is the deploy.

The whole per-site remainder is a config module, three small route pairs, one JSON allowlist and a ten-line workflow.

That is the whole of the parity work. The editor's content box is the article's box because it
renders in the light DOM, in your tree and your cascade, so every rule your site sets already applies and none of them has to be restated.

It loads the editor stack dynamically, so nothing about it reaches a Content page.

Signing in mints a GitHub App installation token scoped to your one repository, with contents read/write and about an hour's life. Three things have to be true before the auth worker will mint it.

Check the whole of it before the first sign-in.

checks that the App is installed on the repository, that the allowlist is committed on the default branch and lists your origin, and that Pages is enabled and serving that origin. Each failure names the worker refusal it would have produced and what to do about it, so a missed step is not something you learn from a failed sign-in.
, not by site. On a shared-origin host —
, where every project page of an account shares one origin — allowlisting the origin authorizes every site served from it. That is fine when they are all yours. A
gives each site its own origin and restores per-site granularity, which is why one is worth setting up before you invite anyone else to edit.
Uncial publishes a reusable workflow that does check, unit tests, build, the zero-CMS-JS gate, upload and deploy to Pages. Your own workflow names the trigger, the permissions and the call:

# .github/workflows/pages.yml
name: Pages
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions: { contents: read, pages: write, id-token: write }
jobs:
  site:
    uses: d-flood/uncial/.github/workflows/static-site.yml@main
    with:
      base-path: /${{ github.event.repository.name }}
Permissions are the caller's: a reusable workflow inherits the calling job's token scopes, so those three have to be declared in your file.

Edit the page in place. It is the same components and the same layout a reader gets.

as it polls the commit's status. The commit link goes to the commit itself. Your edit is now a line in the repository's history, and the deploy that publishes it is your ordinary deploy.
If someone else committed to that document while you were editing, the sha you hold is stale, the write is refused with a 409, and a
conflict banner appears rather than a silent overwrite. It offers three things:

Some sites are edited only by the person holding the checkout. Omitting the
half is the whole of that configuration:
There is no forge, so there is nothing to authorize: no App, no allowlist, no worker, no
. Everything else — the route pairs, the blocks, the schema,
. The local forge reads and writes the checkout through the development-only endpoint the Vite plugin installs.
There is no Save button. On a local checkout the file
writes it that many milliseconds after the last change and there is nothing a save step would reconcile. On a forge, where every keystroke would be a commit, the same field is ignored.
The production build has no Editor variants: the editor routes prerender no entries, and
gates its dynamic imports on a build-time literal, so the editor stack is unreachable and Rollup drops it rather than merely leaving it unrouted.
